# Lecture 4: Conditioning, Bayes' rule, and independence {#b04}

::: {.outcomes}
<span class="label">By the end of Lecture 4, you can</span>

- calculate conditional probabilities and say which group each one refers to,
- rebuild an overall probability from the rates of separate groups,
- update a probability after new evidence with Bayes' rule,
- check whether two events are independent and tell this apart from disjoint.
:::

::: {.driving-question}
<span class="label">Driving question</span>

<p class="dq-context">New information changes our assessment of chances. If you know that a pitch comes from a late season, the chance of a deal changes. The difficulty is to read such a chance the right way round. "Deals among late-season pitches" and "late-season pitches among deals" are different numbers.</p>

You will pitch in a late season. Which of these two sentences tells you how
likely a deal is?

- A. 68.8% of late-season pitches reached an on-air deal.
- B. 57.3% of the pitches that reached a deal came from the late seasons.
:::

::: {.course-phase .phase-before}

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Warm up.** Lecture 2 built the counts table for deals and
seasons from the Shark Tank file. Build it again. The events $D$ (on-air
deal) and $L$ (late season) are defined as in Lecture 2:

```{r}
#| label: b04-prep-table
#| eval: false
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1   # on-air deal
L <- sharks$season >= 9         # late season: Seasons 9-16
table(deal = D, late = L)
```

Then compare, in words only:

- "Among pitches in Seasons 9 to 16, what proportion reached an on-air deal?"
- "Among pitches that reached an on-air deal, what proportion came from
  Seasons 9 to 16?"

For both questions, the number on top of the fraction is the same: the
late-season pitches that reached a deal. The questions differ in the group
that you divide by. Before class, decide for each question which total of
your table goes underneath: the total of the late-season column, or the
total of the deal row. Finally, answer one question on the videos: in
words, what does it mean that two events $A$ and $B$ are independent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your preparation

- The first question divides by the total of the late-season column, 734
  pitches: $505/734\approx 0.688$, or 68.8%.
- The second question divides by the total of the deal row, 882 pitches:
  $505/882\approx 0.573$, or 57.3%.

The same 505 pitches give two different shares because the group you divide
by differs. Two events are independent when knowing that one occurred does
not change the probability of the other, for example
$P(A\mid B)=P(A)$.
:::

**Predict.** Answer this question before you come to class. A venture fund
receives many pitches by email, and only 10% of them end in a deal with the
fund. To save time, the fund tests an AI tool that marks some pitches as
promising. We call such a mark a flag. Among the pitches that later reach a
deal, the tool flags 80%. Among the pitches that do not reach a deal, it
also flags 20%. Now the tool flags one new pitch. How likely is it that this
pitch reaches a deal: near 80%, near 50%, or near 30%? Do not calculate.
Choose one answer and write down your reason in one sentence. You find the
answer in the section "Bayes' rule: count first, formula second".

:::

## Lecture material

Lecture 2 gave each event one probability, computed from all pitches in the
file. In practice you usually know something extra about a case: the season
of a pitch, the sector of a startup, or a signal from a screening tool. Such
information should change your assessment of the chances. This lecture shows
how to update a probability when new information arrives, and how to avoid
reading the update the wrong way round, which is the trap in the driving
question.

The lecture builds four tools on one counts table. Conditional probability
gives the chance of an event within a group. The law of total probability
rebuilds an overall chance from the chances within groups. Bayes' rule turns
a conditional probability around. Independence describes the case in which
new information does not change the chance at all.

### Start with a founder's question

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A founder hears that most deals on the show come from the later seasons. The
founder concludes that a pitch in a later season is likely to end in a deal.
Is that the same statement? Here are two sentences about the 1,441 pitches in
the Shark Tank file:

- **Sentence A.** "68.8% of late-season pitches reached an on-air deal."
- **Sentence B.** "57.3% of the pitches that reached a deal came from the
  late seasons."

Both sentences use the same 505 records: the late-season pitches that
reached a deal. But they answer different questions and give different
numbers. This lecture shows what each sentence claims. Later, the lecture
uses the same idea in another situation: a venture fund that screens the
pitches it receives with an AI tool.

### One table, five probabilities {#b04-one-table}

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The starting point is the counts table from Lecture 2. The code builds the
events $D$ (on-air deal, `deal_on_show`) and $L$ (late season, `season` 9 or
higher) as before. Run it yourself:

```{r}
#| label: b04-counts-table
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1   # on-air deal
L <- sharks$season >= 9         # late season: Seasons 9-16
table(deal = D, late = L)
```

The output has two rows (`deal` FALSE or TRUE) and two columns (`late`
FALSE or TRUE). Each number counts the pitches with that combination. For
example, 505 pitches are from a late season and reached a deal. The same
table with labels and with row and column totals:

|                    | Early ($L^c$, Seasons 1 to 8) | Late ($L$, Seasons 9 to 16) | Total |
|--------------------|---------------------:|-------------------:|------:|
| **No deal** ($D^c$) | 330 | 229 | **559** |
| **Deal** ($D$)      | 377 | 505 | **882** |
| **Total**           | **707** | **734** | **1441** |

Each of the five quantities below is a fraction of two counts. Before you
read on, find in the table the count that goes on top and the count that
goes underneath.

1. $P(D)$, the probability that a pitch reached a deal.
2. $P(L)$, the probability that a pitch is from the late seasons.
3. $P(D\cap L)$, the probability that a pitch is from the late seasons and
   reached a deal.
4. Among late-season pitches, the share that reached a deal.
5. Among pitches that reached a deal, the share that came from the late
   seasons.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your denominators

1. $P(D)$: 882 deal records out of all 1,441 records.
2. $P(L)$: 734 late-season records out of all 1,441 records.
3. $P(D\cap L)$: 505 late-season deal records out of all 1,441 records.
4. Among late-season pitches, the share with a deal: 505 late-season deal
   records out of the 734 late-season records.
5. Among deal pitches, the share from the late seasons: 505 late-season deal
   records out of the 882 deal records.

The first three all divide by 1,441, the number of all pitches. The last two
divide by a part of the table. A share within a part of the table is called
a conditional probability. The next section defines it.
:::

### Conditional probability

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MPRKc4UPoJk">02.2 Conditional Probabilities</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A probability describes how uncertain you
are, given what you know. When you learn something new, some outcomes are
no longer possible. If you know that a pitch comes from a late season, the
early-season pitches can no longer be the one you are looking at. A good
probability model drops these outcomes and spreads the full probability of
1 over the outcomes that are left. This updating is what items 4 and 5 above
ask for: what is the probability of one event if you already know that
another event happens?

You answer such a question in two steps. First, keep only the pitches that
match what you know, for item 4 the 734 late-season pitches. This group is
called the **reference class**. Second, take the share of the reference
class in which the event happens. For item 4, 505 of the 734 late-season
pitches reached a deal. Restricting attention to a reference class is
called **conditioning** on it. @fig-b04-conditioning shows both steps as
areas.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-conditioning
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| fig-cap: "Conditioning shrinks the sample space and rescales it. Panel 1: all 1,441 pitches as a square of area 1. The early column (green) and the late column (orange) have widths P(L^c) and P(L). The solid parts are the deals, so the deals D are split across the two columns. Panel 2: given L, only the late column is left. It is stretched to the full width, so its area is 1 again, and the solid part now has area P(D | L). Panel 3: given D, only the two solid deal parts are left, rescaled to fill the square, and the late part has area P(L | D)."
#| fig-alt: "Three square panels. Panel 1 shows all pitches split into a green early column and an orange late column, each with a solid lower part for deals: 377 early deals, 505 late deals, 330 early pitches without a deal and 229 late pitches without a deal. Panel 2 shows only the late column stretched to the full square: the solid deal part covers 68.8 percent. Panel 3 shows only the deals stretched to the full square: the early part covers 42.7 percent and the late part 57.3 percent."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
p_early <- mean(!L)                 # width of the early column
rate_early <- mean(D[!L])           # deal rate among early pitches
rate_late <- mean(D[L])             # deal rate among late pitches
late_among_deals <- mean(L[D])      # share of late pitches among deals
pct <- function(x) paste0(format(round(100 * x, 1), nsmall = 1), "%")

panels <- c("1. All 1,441 pitches",
            "2. Given L: keep the 734 late pitches",
            "3. Given D: keep the 882 deal pitches")
rects <- data.frame(
  panel = factor(panels[c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)], levels = panels),
  xmin = c(0, p_early, 0, p_early, 0, 0, 0, 1 - late_among_deals),
  xmax = c(p_early, 1, p_early, 1, 1, 1, 1 - late_among_deals, 1),
  ymin = 0,
  ymax = c(1, 1, rate_early, rate_late, 1, rate_late, 1, 1),
  period = c("early", "late", "early", "late", "late", "late", "early", "late"),
  solid = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
labels <- data.frame(
  panel = factor(panels[c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)], levels = panels),
  x = c(p_early / 2, (1 + p_early) / 2, p_early / 2, (1 + p_early) / 2,
        0.5, 0.5, (1 - late_among_deals) / 2, 1 - late_among_deals / 2),
  y = c(rate_early / 2, rate_late / 2, (1 + rate_early) / 2,
        (1 + rate_late) / 2, rate_late / 2, (1 + rate_late) / 2, 0.5, 0.5),
  text = c("deal,\nearly\n377", "deal,\nlate\n505",
           "no deal,\nearly\n330", "no deal,\nlate\n229",
           paste0("deal\n505 of 734\n= ", pct(rate_late)),
           paste0("no deal\n229 of 734\n= ", pct(1 - rate_late)),
           paste0("early\n377 of 882\n= ", pct(1 - late_among_deals)),
           paste0("late\n505 of 882\n= ", pct(late_among_deals))),
  colour = c("white", "white", "#17324D", "#17324D",
             "white", "#17324D", "white", "white")
)

ggplot() +
  geom_rect(data = rects,
            aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax,
                fill = period, alpha = solid),
            colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(x = x, y = y, label = text),
            colour = labels$colour, size = 3.1, lineheight = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(early = "#009E73", late = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 0.25, `TRUE` = 0.9)) +
  coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold",
                                  margin = margin(b = 6)),
        panel.border = element_rect(colour = "#17324D", fill = NA,
                                    linewidth = 0.8),
        panel.spacing = unit(1.2, "lines"))
```

Read @fig-b04-conditioning from left to right. Panel 1 shows what you know
before any extra information. The square stands for all 1,441 pitches, so
its area is 1. The deals are split across both periods: 377 early deals and
505 late deals. Panel 2 shows what happens when you learn that the pitch is
from a late season. The early column drops out, because it is no longer
possible. What is left, the late column, is stretched to fill the whole
square, so the probabilities add up to 1 again. The solid part now covers
68.8% of the square. That is the deal probability given a late season.
Panel 3 conditions on the other event. It keeps only the 882 deals and
stretches them to fill the square. The late part now covers 57.3%. Panels 2
and 3 start from the same 505 late-season deals but divide them by different
groups, so they give different numbers.

The symbol for this is a vertical bar, read as "given". Item 4 is written
$P(D\mid L)$, "the probability of $D$ given $L$". Item 5 is written
$P(L\mid D)$. The event after the bar is always the reference class.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Conditional probability.** The probability that event $A$ happens, given
that event $B$ happens. For events $A$ and $B$ with $P(B)>0$,

$$P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.$$

In words: keep only the outcomes in $B$, then take the share of them that
are also in $A$.
:::

The formula does the same two steps as the count. For item 4,

$$P(D\mid L)=\frac{P(D\cap L)}{P(L)}
=\frac{505/1441}{734/1441}=\frac{505}{734}.$$

The reference class gives the denominator. Dividing by $P(B)$ rescales
the probabilities inside $B$ so that they add up to 1 again. This is the
stretching step from panel 1 to panel 2 of @fig-b04-conditioning.

For a fixed event $B$, conditional probabilities follow all three rules from
Lecture 2. So every rule that Lecture 2 derived from them also holds inside
the reference class. The condition is that the event after the bar stays the
same in the whole calculation. Two examples follow. The first is
the complement rule, $P(A^c\mid B)=1-P(A\mid B)$. Among late-season pitches,
the share without a deal is

$$P(D^c\mid L)=1-P(D\mid L)=1-\frac{505}{734}=\frac{229}{734}\approx 0.312.$$

The second is the addition rule. For two events $A$ and $C$ and the same
reference class $B$,

$$P(A\cup C\mid B)=P(A\mid B)+P(C\mid B)-P(A\cap C\mid B).$$

Some calculations mix different reference classes, for example $P(A\mid B)$
and $P(A\mid B^c)$. For these you need the law of total probability,
which a later section explains.

::: {#exm-b04-conditional}
## Worked example: what each of the two sentences means

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Sentence A asks about $P(D\mid L)$.** Conditioning on $L$ means that you
hide everything except the Late column:

|                    | Early | **Late ($L$)** |
|--------------------|------:|---------------:|
| No deal            | · | **229** |
| Deal               | · | **505** |
| Total              | · | **734** |

Within that one column, 505 of 734 records are deals:

$$P(D\mid L)=\frac{505}{734}\approx 0.688.$$

**Sentence B asks about $P(L\mid D)$.** Conditioning on $D$ means that you
hide everything except the Deal row:

|                    | Early | Late | Total |
|--------------------|------:|-----:|------:|
| No deal            | · | · | · |
| **Deal ($D$)**     | **377** | **505** | **882** |

Within that one row, 505 of 882 records are late-season:

$$P(L\mid D)=\frac{505}{882}\approx 0.573.$$

The numerator is 505 in both calculations: the same cell of the table. The
denominators differ, and so do the questions. Sentence A looks only at the
734 late-season pitches. Sentence B looks only at the 882 deal pitches.
:::

To match a sentence with its number, look at the words after "of" or
"among". Sentence A, "68.8% of late-season pitches reached an on-air deal",
names the late-season pitches as the group, so it is
$P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 68.8\%$. Sentence B, "57.3% of the pitches that
reached a deal came from the late seasons", names the deals as the group,
so it is $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 57.3\%$. A report that says "68.8% of
deal pitches came from late seasons" has put the right number into the
wrong sentence.

The same two numbers in R. In the code, `D` and `L` are lists of 1,441
TRUE/FALSE values, one for each pitch. Square brackets select entries: `D[L]`
keeps the deal values of only those pitches where `L` is TRUE, so it is the
list of 734 late-season pitches. This is the step that keeps only the
reference class. `mean()` of TRUE/FALSE values is the share of TRUE values,
just as the mean of a 0/1 variable is its share of 1s. So `mean(D[L])` is
the share of deals among late-season pitches. In the same way, `L[D]` keeps
the 882 deal pitches and `mean(L[D])` is the share of them from a late
season. The first output counts the size of each reference class, with
`sum()`, which counts the TRUE values. The second output gives the two
shares:

```{r}
#| label: b04-conditionals
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
c(n_late = sum(L), n_deal = sum(D))
c(
  P_deal_given_late = mean(D[L]),
  P_late_given_deal = mean(L[D])
)
```

R confirms both reference classes (734 late-season pitches and 882 deals)
and both shares: 0.688 for Sentence A and 0.573 for Sentence B. For
comparison, the deal rate among all pitches is $882/1441\approx 0.612$. So
late-season pitches have a deal rate about 7.6 percentage points higher than
all pitches together.

### The multiplication rule

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ugzs7dgQ-JE">02.6 The Multiplication Rule</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Often you know a rate within a group and the
size of the group, but not how often both things happen together. A bank,
for example, may know that 30% of its loans go to small businesses and that
5% of those loans are not repaid. The share of all loans that are
small-business loans and not repaid is then $0.05\times 0.30=0.015$, or 1.5%
of all loans. The multiplication rule makes this step general.

The probability of an intersection, $P(A\cap B)$, is also called a **joint
probability**: both events happen together. Multiply both sides of the
definition of conditional probability by $P(B)$. The result is the
**multiplication rule**. It builds a joint probability from a conditional
one:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B).$$

The same holds with the roles of $A$ and $B$ exchanged, because $A\cap B$
and $B\cap A$ are the same event:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)=P(B\mid A)\,P(A).$$

This line explains why the two sentences share a numerator and have
different denominators. Both products equal $505/1441$, but each one uses a
different reference class.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Try it: verify the joint probability two ways

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Use the counts table of the section "One
table, five probabilities" to check the equation above for $D$ (on-air deal)
and $L$ (late season).

*Step 1 (given).* The direct way: $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$.

*Step 2 (given).* The first product:
$P(D\mid L)\,P(L)=\dfrac{505}{734}\cdot\dfrac{734}{1441}$. The 734
cancels. Cancel it and confirm that $505/1441$ is left.

*Step 3 (you).* Write the second product, $P(L\mid D)\,P(D)$, as two
fractions from the table. Show that it also equals $505/1441$.

*Step 4 (you).* Confirm all three ways in R.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$P(L\mid D)\,P(D)=\dfrac{505}{882}\cdot\dfrac{882}{1441}=\dfrac{505}{1441}
\approx 0.350$. The 882 cancels, just as the 734 did.

The R code computes the joint probability in the three ways. `mean(D & L)`
is the share of pitches that are both deals and late-season. The other two
lines multiply a conditional share by the share of its reference class. All
three outputs are 0.350: 35% of all pitches are late-season deals, whichever
way you compute it.

```{r}
#| label: b04-multiplication
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
c(
  direct_joint            = mean(D & L),
  cond_on_late_times_base = mean(D[L]) * mean(L),
  cond_on_deal_times_base = mean(L[D]) * mean(D)
)
```
:::
:::

The multiplication rule is the building block of the next two tools. The
law of total probability adds up several joint probabilities, and Bayes'
rule divides one joint probability by a total.

### The law of total probability

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8odFouBR2wE">02.7 Total Probability Theorem</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Data often come as rates for separate
groups: the deal rate in each period of the show, the repayment rate in each
segment of a loan portfolio, or the conversion rate in each sales channel.
A decision may still need the overall rate. The law of total probability
combines the group rates into one overall rate.

Lecture 2 introduced a partition: events that do not overlap and together
cover every outcome. The early seasons and the late seasons are a partition
of the pitches. You can rebuild an overall probability from the parts of a
partition in three steps. Take the conditional probability of $A$ within
each part. Multiply it by the probability of that part, which gives a joint
probability. Then add the joint probabilities.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Law of total probability.** For a partition $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ with every
$P(B_i)>0$,

$$P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(A\mid B_i)\,P(B_i).$$

In words: the overall probability of $A$ is a weighted average of its
probabilities within the groups. The weight of each group is the probability
of that group.
:::

With only two groups, $B$ and its complement $B^c$, the sum has two terms:

$$P(A)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)+P(A\mid B^c)\,P(B^c).$$

::: {#exm-b04-total}
## Worked example: rebuilding P(D) from the deal rates of the two periods

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The early and late events $L^c$ and $L$ form a partition, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(D)&=P(D\mid L^c)\,P(L^c)+P(D\mid L)\,P(L)\\
&=\frac{377}{707}\cdot\frac{707}{1441}
+\frac{505}{734}\cdot\frac{734}{1441}\\
&=\frac{377+505}{1441}=\frac{882}{1441}\approx 0.612.
\end{aligned}
$$

Two kinds of number appear here. $377/707\approx 0.533$ and
$505/734\approx 0.688$ are the deal rates within each period.
$707/1441\approx 0.491$ and $734/1441\approx 0.509$ are the weights: the
share of all pitches that falls in each period. The overall deal probability
is a weighted average of the two rates. So it must lie between 0.533 and
0.688, and it is a little closer to the rate of the larger group.
:::

In R, `mean(D[!L])` is the deal rate among early pitches (`!L` means "not
late"), and `mean(!L)` is the share of early pitches. The second line
multiplies each rate by its weight and adds the two products:

```{r}
#| label: b04-total-probability
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
c(
  direct       = mean(D),
  from_periods = mean(D[!L]) * mean(!L) + mean(D[L]) * mean(L)
)
```

Both outputs are 0.612. Rebuilding the overall deal probability from the
two periods gives exactly the share of deals among all pitches, as the law
promises.

Panel 1 of @fig-b04-conditioning shows the same calculation as areas. The
width of each column is the probability of that period, the weight: 0.491
for the early and 0.509 for the late seasons. The height of the solid part
is the deal rate within that period: 0.533 and 0.688. So the area of each
solid part is width times height, which is a joint probability. For the
late seasons this is $0.509\times 0.688\approx 0.350$, and for the early
seasons $0.491\times 0.533\approx 0.262$. The two solid parts do not
overlap, so $P(D)$ is their total area, $0.262+0.350=0.612$. In the figure
you can also see why the overall rate lies between the two group rates.
Flattening the two solid parts to one common height that keeps their total
area gives a height of 0.612, below the late part and above the early part.
The law of total probability returns in the next section, where it gives
the denominator of Bayes' rule.

### Bayes' rule: count first, formula second

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kz2tvO_ZAKI">02.8 Bayes' Rule</a>.</p>

Many business decisions start from a signal: a flag from a screening tool,
a positive review, or a click on an ad. The quality of a signal is usually
described the other way round, as the share of good cases that show the
signal. The decision needs the share of good cases among those that show
the signal. Bayes' rule turns the one into the other.

Return to the prediction question from before class. It is about another
situation than the Shark Tank show, with invented numbers. A venture fund
receives many pitches from founders by email. Most of them never lead to an
investment: only 10% end in a deal with the fund. To save time, the fund
uses an AI tool that reads each pitch and flags (marks) the pitches that it
considers likely to reach a deal. A tool that sorts cases into two groups in
this way is called a classifier. Three numbers describe it:

- the **base rate**: 10% of the pitches that the fund receives reach a deal,
- the **sensitivity**: among actual deals, 80% get flagged,
  $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})=0.80$,
- the **false-positive rate**: among non-deals, 20% still get flagged,
  $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{no deal})=0.20$.

A pitch has just been flagged. How likely is a deal now: near 80%, 50%,
or 30%? Count first, and use the formula afterwards.

::: {#exm-b04-bayes-tree}
## Worked example: 1,000 imaginary pitches

Imagine 1,000 pitches and apply the three numbers to them one after the
other, as in @fig-b04-bayes-tree.

1. **Split by the base rate.** Of 1,000 pitches, 100 are deals and 900 are
   not.
2. **Flag the deals.** Sensitivity 80%: of the 100 deals, 80 are flagged.
3. **Flag some non-deals too.** False-positive rate 20%: of the 900
   non-deals, 180 are flagged.
4. **Collect the flagged pitches.** In total $80+180=260$ pitches have a flag,
   and only 80 of them are deals:

$$P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=\frac{80}{260}\approx 0.31.$$

The classifier finds 80% of deals, but fewer than a third of the flagged
pitches are deals. The tree shows the reason. The 900 non-deals are a large group, so
even a 20% false-positive rate produces 180 false flags. That is more than
double the 80 true flags. A flag moves the deal probability from 10% to 31%.
This is real evidence, but it is far from certainty.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-bayes-tree
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Tree of counts for 1,000 imaginary pitches. Orange boxes are the flagged pitches: 80 + 180 = 260 flags in total, of which only 80 are deals, so P(deal | flag) = 80/260, about 31%."
#| fig-alt: "A tree that starts with 1,000 pitches, splits into 100 deals and 900 non-deals, and then into flagged and not flagged: 80 flagged and 20 not flagged deals, 180 flagged and 720 not flagged non-deals. The 80 and 180 flagged boxes are highlighted in orange, with 260 flagged in total."
# draw_count_tree() draws a tree of counts. The later trees in this
# lecture reuse it.
draw_count_tree <- function(root, root_label, mid, mid_labels, ends,
                            end_labels, branch_labels, side_text = "") {
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par))
  par(mar = c(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.3, 9.7), axes = FALSE,
       xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  draw_node <- function(x, y, top, bottom, fill = "white",
                        border = "#17324D", lwd = 1.4, w = 1.05, h = 0.78) {
    rect(x - w, y - h, x + w, y + h, col = fill, border = border, lwd = lwd)
    text(x, y + 0.26, top, font = 2, cex = 1.0, col = "#17324D")
    text(x, y - 0.30, bottom, cex = 0.8, col = "#5B6976")
  }
  draw_branch <- function(x1, y1, x2, y2, label, above = TRUE) {
    segments(x1, y1, x2, y2, col = "#9AA7B2", lwd = 1.6)
    text((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2 + if (above) 0.32 else -0.32,
         label, cex = 0.76, col = "#5B6976")
  }
  # branches first, then boxes on top
  draw_branch(2.45, 5.35, 3.55, 7.15, branch_labels[1])
  draw_branch(2.45, 4.65, 3.55, 2.85, branch_labels[2], above = FALSE)
  draw_branch(5.65, 7.75, 6.95, 8.45, branch_labels[3])
  draw_branch(5.65, 7.05, 6.95, 6.35, branch_labels[4], above = FALSE)
  draw_branch(5.65, 2.95, 6.95, 3.65, branch_labels[5])
  draw_branch(5.65, 2.25, 6.95, 1.55, branch_labels[6], above = FALSE)
  draw_node(1.35, 5.0, root, root_label, w = 1.15)
  draw_node(4.6, 7.4, mid[1], mid_labels[1])
  draw_node(4.6, 2.6, mid[2], mid_labels[2])
  # orange boxes: the cases with the signal
  draw_node(8.0, 8.6, ends[1], end_labels[1], fill = "#FDE5C1",
            border = "#D55E00", lwd = 2.2)
  draw_node(8.0, 6.2, ends[2], end_labels[2], fill = "#F4F7F9",
            border = "#9AA7B2")
  draw_node(8.0, 3.8, ends[3], end_labels[3], fill = "#FDE5C1",
            border = "#D55E00", lwd = 2.2)
  draw_node(8.0, 1.4, ends[4], end_labels[4], fill = "#F4F7F9",
            border = "#9AA7B2")
  text(9.55, 6.2, side_text, cex = 0.82, col = "#D55E00")
}

draw_count_tree(
  root = "1,000", root_label = "pitches",
  mid = c("100", "900"), mid_labels = c("deal", "no deal"),
  ends = c("80", "20", "180", "720"),
  end_labels = c("flagged", "not flagged", "flagged", "not flagged"),
  branch_labels = c("10% deal", "90% no deal", "80% flagged", "20% not",
                    "20% flagged", "80% not"),
  side_text = "260\nflagged\nin total"
)
```

Now the formula. The question turns a condition around. We describe the
quality of the classifier with $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})$, but the
person who makes the decision needs $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})$. The multiplication rule gives
the numerator, and the law of total probability gives the denominator.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Bayes' rule.** A formula that turns a conditional probability around: from
$P(A\mid B)$ to $P(B\mid A)$. For events $A$ and $B$ with positive
probability,

$$P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}.$$

When $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ form a partition, you can write out the denominator
$P(A)$ with the law of total probability:

$$P(B_i\mid A)=\frac{P(A\mid B_i)\,P(B_i)}
{\sum_{j=1}^{k} P(A\mid B_j)\,P(B_j)}.$$
:::

For the classifier, the partition is deal and no deal:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})
&=\frac{0.80\times 0.10}{0.80\times 0.10+0.20\times 0.90}\\
&=\frac{0.08}{0.08+0.18}=\frac{0.08}{0.26}\approx 0.308.
\end{aligned}
$$

Every term is a branch of the tree, divided by 1,000:

| Formula term | Value | Tree count |
|---|---:|---|
| $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{deal})\,P(\text{deal})$ | $0.08$ | the 80 flagged deals |
| $P(\text{flag}\mid\text{no deal})\,P(\text{no deal})$ | $0.18$ | the 180 flagged non-deals |
| the denominator (total probability of a flag) | $0.26$ | all 260 flagged pitches |

The formula is a short way to write the tree. Drawing a tree and counting is
a good way to solve a Bayes question. Use an imaginary total that is
easy to calculate with, such as 1,000.
The tree and the formula always give the same answer.

Bayes' rule also works on the Shark Tank events. Starting from
$P(D\mid L)$, it gives $P(L\mid D)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(L\mid D)&=\frac{P(D\mid L)\,P(L)}{P(D)}\\
&=\frac{(505/734)(734/1441)}{882/1441}=\frac{505}{882}\approx 0.573.
\end{aligned}
$$

The R check computes the same formula and compares it with the direct count
from the table. The first line plugs $P(D\mid L)$, $P(L)$ and $P(D)$ into
Bayes' rule. The second line takes the share of late-season pitches among
the deals directly:

```{r}
#| label: b04-bayes
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
bayes_late_given_deal <- mean(D[L]) * mean(L) / mean(D)
c(
  from_bayes = bayes_late_given_deal,
  from_table = mean(L[D])
)
```

Both numbers are 0.573: Bayes' rule turns the 68.8% of Sentence A into the
57.3% of Sentence B. With a counts table at hand you can always count
directly. Bayes' rule is needed when, as for the venture fund, you only know
the rates in one direction and the base rate.

### Independence of events

<p class="concept-video"><strong>MIT explanation (review):</strong>
<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w423ypsUHf0">03.3 Independence of Two Events</a>.</p>

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Sometimes knowing that one event happened
tells you nothing about another event. This case matters in practice. A
signal that is unrelated to the outcome in this way is useless for
screening, however often it appears. In finance, an investor who holds
several startups hopes that their failures are unrelated, so that one
failure does not make the others more likely. Conditional probability makes
the idea precise.

::: {.definition-box}
<span class="label">Definition</span>

**Independent events.** Events $A$ and $B$ are independent when learning that
$B$ happened does not change the probability of $A$. For $P(B)>0$,

$$P(A\mid B)=P(A).$$

The same condition in **product form**:

$$P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B).$$
:::

The product form follows when you multiply both sides of the first equation
by $P(B)$. It treats $A$ and $B$ in the same way, and it also works when an
event has probability zero. Events that are not independent are called
dependent.

::: {#exm-b04-independence}
## Worked example: are D and L independent?

Check both forms with the numbers from the counts table.

With conditioning: $P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688$, while
$P(D)=882/1441\approx 0.612$. Late-season pitches have a higher deal rate
than all pitches together, so $D$ and $L$ are not independent.

With the product form: $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$, while
$$P(D)\,P(L)=\frac{882}{1441}\cdot\frac{734}{1441}\approx 0.612\times0.509\approx 0.312.$$
The joint probability is larger than the product. This
says the same thing: deals and late seasons occur together more often than
they would under independence.
:::

```{r}
#| label: b04-independence
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
L <- sharks$season >= 9
c(
  P_D_given_L  = mean(D[L]),
  P_D          = mean(D),
  P_D_and_L    = mean(D & L),
  P_D_times_P_L = mean(D) * mean(L)
)
```

The R output repeats both checks. The first pair compares $P(D\mid L)=0.688$
with $P(D)=0.612$: late-season pitches have a deal rate 7.6 percentage
points higher, about an eighth of the overall rate. The second
pair compares $P(D\cap L)=0.350$ with $P(D)\,P(L)=0.312$. Both pairs differ,
so both checks agree that $D$ and $L$ are dependent.

#### Disjoint is not the same as independent

The two words sound alike, but they describe very different situations.

|  | Disjoint events | Independent events |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | $A$ and $B$ never happen together | Learning that $B$ happened does not change the chance of $A$ |
| Condition | $P(A\cap B)=0$ | $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)$ |
| Example | $A$: the pitch is from an early season. $B$: the same pitch is from a late season. | $A$: the first toss of a fair coin lands heads. $B$: the second toss lands heads. |

Take the early and late events $L^c$ and $L$. They are disjoint: no pitch is
in both periods. Before you know anything, the probability of a late season
is $P(L)\approx 0.509$. Now you learn that the pitch is from an early
season. Then it cannot be from a late season, so $P(L\mid L^c)=0$. The new
information has moved the probability from about 51% to 0%. That is the
largest change possible, so the two events are as far from independent as
events can be. The product form shows the same: $P(L^c\cap L)=0$, while
$P(L^c)\,P(L)\approx 0.491\times 0.509\approx 0.25$.

The same reasoning holds for any two disjoint events with positive
probability. Knowing that one happened makes the other impossible, so they
can never be independent. For two coin tosses it is the other way round.
Both can land heads, and the first toss tells you nothing about the second.

Independence closes the toolbox of this lecture. One more use of conditional
probability is so common in business reports that it deserves its own
section: comparing the success rates of groups. The next section shows that
such a comparison is a set of conditional probabilities, and why shares and
not counts must be compared.

### Second application: deal rates by team composition

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Founders and investors often compare groups:
do pitches by some kinds of teams reach deals more often than others? Such a
comparison is a set of conditional probabilities, one for each group. The
variable `pitcher_gender_group` in the Shark Tank file puts each team that
pitches into one of four groups: `all_men`, `all_women`, `mixed`, or
`unknown`. The deal rate within a category is a conditional probability,
$P(D\mid \text{category})$, with the category as reference class.

The code keeps the pitches with a known category. `table()` counts the
pitches in each category with and without a deal. `tapply()` splits the
deal indicator by category and takes the mean within each category, which
is the share of deals in that category:

```{r}
#| label: b04-team-deal-rates
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
D <- sharks$deal_on_show == 1
known_gender <- sharks$pitcher_gender_group != "unknown"
gender_labels <- c("all_men", "all_women", "mixed")
team <- factor(sharks$pitcher_gender_group[known_gender],
               levels = gender_labels)

table(team = team, deal = D[known_gender])
gender_deal_rates <- tapply(sharks$deal_on_show[known_gender], team, mean)
gender_deal_rates
```

Adding each row of the table, all-men teams made $324+449=773$ pitches,
all-women teams $140+245=385$, and mixed teams $93+183=276$. The rates are 58.1% for all-men, 63.6% for all-women,
and 66.3% for mixed teams.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-team-deal-rates
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the R code for this figure"
#| fig-cap: "Share of pitches with an on-air deal by team category (`pitcher_gender_group`), among the 1,434 Shark Tank pitches with a known category. Each bar is a percentage within its own category: P(deal | category). The three rates lie between 58% and 67%."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of the share of pitches with an on-air deal for three team categories. All-men teams have 58.1 percent, all-women teams 63.6 percent, and mixed teams 66.3 percent."
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known_gender <- sharks$pitcher_gender_group != "unknown"
gender_labels <- c("all_men", "all_women", "mixed")
gender_deal_rates <- tapply(
  sharks$deal_on_show[known_gender],
  factor(sharks$pitcher_gender_group[known_gender], levels = gender_labels),
  mean
)
gender_counts <- table(
  factor(sharks$pitcher_gender_group[known_gender], levels = gender_labels)
)
rates_df <- data.frame(
  team = paste0(c("All-men", "All-women", "Mixed"),
                "\n(n = ", as.integer(gender_counts), ")"),
  deal_rate = as.numeric(gender_deal_rates)
)
rates_df$team <- factor(rates_df$team, levels = rates_df$team)

ggplot(rates_df, aes(x = team, y = deal_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.85, colour = "white",
           width = 0.62) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(100 * deal_rate, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.6, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.75),
                     breaks = seq(0, 0.75, by = 0.15),
                     labels = paste0(seq(0, 75, by = 15), "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Source classification of pitching team",
       y = "Pitches with an on-air deal") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )
```

@fig-b04-team-deal-rates shows three conditional proportions, each with its
own denominator. The 63.6% bar means that 63.6% of the 385 pitches by
all-women teams reached an on-air deal.

Why compare shares and not simply the numbers of deals? The counts table
shows 449 deals for all-men teams, 245 for all-women teams and 183 for mixed
teams. Mixed teams have the fewest deals, but only because they made the
fewest pitches. Their share of deals is the highest. Dividing by the size of
each group puts all three groups on the same scale: deals per 100 pitches of
that group. On this scale, mixed teams reached a deal 8.2 percentage points
more often than all-men teams, and all-women teams 5.6 percentage points
more often. Relative to the all-men rate of 58.1%, these differences are
about 14% and 10%.

::: {.caveat-box}
<span class="label">What a conditional probability can and cannot say</span>

- Turning a condition around changes the number. Neither number shows a
  cause. 68.8% of late-season pitches got a deal. That does not mean that late
  seasons cause deals.
- The team comparison uses the broad groups of presenters that the data
  source defined. It also uses only pitches that the producers selected.
- The numbers for the AI tool of the venture fund are invented. If they were
  realistic for a real fund, the fund should conclude that about two out of
  three flagged pitches never lead to a deal. A real fund would need its own
  base rate and its own flag rates to draw this conclusion.

**What you can do with it:** before you act on a signal, look up the base
rate, the share of all cases that have the outcome you are looking for. In
the venture fund example only 10% of pitches reach a deal. The 900
non-deals then produce 180 false flags, more than the 80 true flags from
the 100 deals. Whenever the base rate is low, many signals are false
alarms. So treat a signal as a reason for a closer look, for example a
short call with the founder, and not as a final decision.
:::

### Answering the driving question

The driving question asked which sentence tells you how likely a deal is
when you pitch in a late season. The answer is Sentence A. It is
$P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx0.688$, with the late-season pitches as reference
class: about 69% of them reached a deal. Sentence B is
$P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx0.573$, with the deals as reference class. It
tells you how the deals are split over the seasons, not how likely a deal
is for your pitch. Both sentences are correct and use the same 505 records,
but they answer different questions. The typical error is to use the number
of one sentence in the other.

As a founder who pitches in a late season, you might expect a chance of
about 69% to leave with an on-air deal. That is 7.6 percentage points above
the 61.2% for all seasons together. This expectation rests on two
assumptions: that your pitch is like a typical late-season pitch in the
file, and that the show keeps selecting and judging pitches as it did in
Seasons 9 to 16. It does not say that pitching later causes a deal.

The venture fund example shows the same trap with a signal. A flag from the
fund's AI tool tells less than its 80% sensitivity suggests. With a 10%
base rate and a 20% false-positive rate, only $80/260\approx 31\%$ of
flagged pitches reach a deal. Among flagged pitches the probability of a
deal is 31% instead of 10%, and not more.

::: {.founder-box}
<span class="label">A founder's decision (invented example)</span>

Your venture sells boxes of prepared meals by subscription, and you give away
free trial boxes. One in ten trial customers becomes a subscriber. You notice
a signal: 80% of later subscribers open your follow-up email, and 20% of the
others open it too. You could call trial customers to convince them. A phone
call costs you 2 euros of your time, and a subscriber is worth 30 euros to
you. Whom should you call: the customers who opened the email, the others,
or everybody?

Try it yourself first.

1. Draw a tree of counts for 1,000 trial customers: subscribers or not, then
   opened the email or not.
2. Calculate the share of subscribers among the customers who opened the
   email, and among those who did not.
3. Calculate the expected value of one call in each group, and compare it
   with the cost of 2 euros.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See the solution

1. Of 1,000 trial customers, 100 become subscribers and 900 do not. Of the
   100 subscribers, $0.80\times100=80$ open the email. Of the 900 others,
   $0.20\times900=180$ open it. So $80+180=260$ customers open the email
   and 740 do not. @fig-b04-subscriber-tree shows the tree.
2. Among the openers, $80/260\approx0.31$ become subscribers. Among the 740
   who did not open, $100-80=20$ become subscribers: $20/740\approx0.03$.
3. A call to an opener is worth $(80/260)\times30\approx9.23$ euros on
   average, more than the 2 euros that it costs. A call to a customer who
   did not open is worth $(20/740)\times30\approx0.81$ euros on average, less
   than the 2 euros.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-subscriber-tree
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Tree of counts for 1,000 imaginary trial customers. Orange boxes are the customers who opened the follow-up email: 80 + 180 = 260 in total, of which 80 become subscribers, so P(subscriber | opened) = 80/260, about 31%."
#| fig-alt: "A tree that starts with 1,000 trial customers, splits into 100 subscribers and 900 non-subscribers, and then into opened and not opened: 80 opened and 20 not opened among subscribers, 180 opened and 720 not opened among non-subscribers. The 80 and 180 boxes are highlighted in orange, with 260 opened in total."
# draw_count_tree() is defined in the code of the tree of 1,000 pitches
draw_count_tree(
  root = "1,000", root_label = "trial customers",
  mid = c("100", "900"), mid_labels = c("subscriber", "no subscriber"),
  ends = c("80", "20", "180", "720"),
  end_labels = c("opened", "not opened", "opened", "not opened"),
  branch_labels = c("10% subscribe", "90% do not", "80% open", "20% not",
                    "20% open", "80% not"),
  side_text = "260\nopened\nin total"
)
```

The decision: call the openers and nobody else. This is Bayes' rule at
work: the signal moves the chance of a subscriber from 10% to 31%.
:::
:::

**Next:** You can now update the probability of one event when another
event is known. In practice you are rarely interested in one variable
alone. A founder wants to know how sales move with advertising spending, or
how the equity offered relates to the size of the investment. Such
questions are about relationships between variables. Lecture 5 therefore
looks at two random variables at the same time,
for example the season of a pitch and the equity offered. It introduces two
numbers that measure how two variables change together, the covariance and the
correlation. It also shows what a correlation can and cannot tell you.

:::

::: {.course-phase .phase-after}

## After class

After the lecture, work through all the practice below.

### Read the lecture material

Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture
covered the main points. The text has every step, every example, and all the
code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still
unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.

### Recall questions

1. What is the denominator of $P(A\mid B)$?
2. Why is $P(A\mid B)$ generally different from $P(B\mid A)$?
3. What makes a collection of events a partition?
4. What does the denominator in Bayes' rule calculate?
5. State the two equivalent definitions of independence of events.
6. Can two disjoint events, each with positive probability, be independent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. $P(B)$, the probability of the conditioning event.
2. They condition on different reference classes, so they have different
   denominators.
3. No two parts overlap, and together they make up $\Omega$ (their union is
   $\Omega$).
4. The total probability of the observed evidence, added across all parts of
   the partition.
5. $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ (learning $B$ does not change the probability of $A$),
   and the product form $P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)$.
6. No. Their intersection has probability 0 while the product of their
   probabilities is positive, so the product check fails. Observing one makes
   the other impossible.
:::

### Finish a half-worked example: the Bayes tree

Re-read the worked example with the tree of 1,000 pitches
(@exm-b04-bayes-tree). Then build the tree again for an AI classifier that
flags pitches likely to get a deal, with new numbers. Of the checked
pitches, 20% reach a deal (the base rate). The classifier flags 90% of the
deals (the sensitivity) and 30% of the non-deals (the false-positive
rate).

*Step 1 (given).* Start with 1,000 imaginary pitches: 200 deals, 800
non-deals.

*Step 2 (you).* Fill in the four boxes with a question mark at the end of
the tree in @fig-b04-tree-exercise: the flagged and the unflagged counts in
each branch.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-tree-exercise
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Tree of counts for 1,000 imaginary pitches with the new classifier. The first split is given. Fill in the four boxes on the right. The orange boxes are the flagged pitches."
#| fig-alt: "A tree that starts with 1,000 pitches and splits into 200 deals and 800 non-deals. The branches then split into flagged and not flagged, with 90 percent and 10 percent for deals and 30 percent and 70 percent for non-deals. The four end boxes show question marks."
# draw_count_tree() is defined in the code of the tree of 1,000 pitches
draw_count_tree(
  root = "1,000", root_label = "pitches",
  mid = c("200", "800"), mid_labels = c("deal", "no deal"),
  ends = c("?", "?", "?", "?"),
  end_labels = c("flagged", "not flagged", "flagged", "not flagged"),
  branch_labels = c("20% deal", "80% no deal", "90% flagged", "10% not",
                    "30% flagged", "70% not")
)
```

*Step 3 (you).* Collect the flagged pitches and compute
$P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

Of the 200 deals, 90% are flagged: 180. Of the 800 non-deals, 30% are
flagged: 240. Flagged total $180+240=420$, of which 180 are deals:
$P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=180/420\approx 0.429$. The formula agrees:
$\dfrac{0.90\times 0.20}{0.90\times 0.20+0.30\times 0.80}
=\dfrac{0.18}{0.42}\approx 0.429$.
:::

**On your own.** A more accurate classifier checks a group of pitches in which 5%
reach a deal. Its sensitivity is 90% and its false-positive rate is 10%.
What share of flagged pitches are deals? Use either the tree or the formula.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

With 1,000 pitches: 50 deals, of which 45 are flagged, and 950 non-deals, of
which 95 are flagged. $P(\text{deal}\mid\text{flag})=45/(45+95)=45/140\approx 0.321$.
Even with 90% sensitivity and a low false-positive rate, the 5% base rate
keeps the share of true flags below one third.
:::

### Practice

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Select one of the 1,441 recorded pitches at random. $D$ is the event
of an on-air deal, and $L$ is the event of a late season (Seasons 9 to 16).
Use the counts table of the section
[One table, five probabilities](#b04-one-table).

1. Use the early/late partition to verify
   $$P(D)=P(D\mid L^c)\,P(L^c)+P(D\mid L)\,P(L).$$
2. Calculate and interpret $P(L\mid D)$. Explain why it differs from
   $P(D\mid L)$.
3. Decide by calculation whether $D$ and $L$ are independent, using the
   product form.
4. The events $L^c$ and $L$ are disjoint. Are they independent? Explain in
   one sentence.
5. Consider the 1,434 pitches with a known classification of the team. Of
   the 661 pitches with women represented (all-women or mixed), 428 reached
   an on-air deal. Of the 773 all-men pitches, 449 reached an on-air deal.
   Calculate both conditional deal proportions and interpret the difference.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answers

1. The two products add up to the overall deal probability:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   &(377/707)(707/1441)+(505/734)(734/1441)\\
   &=(377+505)/1441=882/1441\approx 0.612.
   \end{aligned}
   $$
2. $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 0.573$: among deal records, 57.3% came from
   Seasons 9 to 16. It differs from $P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688$ because
   the conditioning event, and so the denominator, is different.
3. $P(D\cap L)=505/1441\approx 0.350$, while
   $P(D)\,P(L)=(882/1441)(734/1441)\approx 0.312$. The two are not equal, so
   $D$ and $L$ are not independent.
4. No: $P(L^c\cap L)=0$ but $P(L^c)\,P(L)\approx 0.25>0$, so the product
   check fails. Disjoint events with positive probability are always
   dependent.
5. $428/661\approx 0.648$ and $449/773\approx 0.581$, a descriptive
   difference of about 6.7 percentage points. The data source defined the
   groups, and the producers chose the pitches for television. The difference does
   not show that the kind of team causes the deal.
:::

### Review questions from past lectures

A variable $Y$ has PMF $p_Y(0)=0.2$, $p_Y(1)=0.5$, and $p_Y(2)=0.3$.
Calculate $E[Y]$ and say in one sentence what the number means. Can
$Y$ ever equal it exactly?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

$E[Y]=0(0.2)+1(0.5)+2(0.3)=1.1$. It is the probability-weighted average of
the possible values, and the long-run average over many repetitions. It does
not have to be a value that the variable can take: here $Y$ is never 1.1.
:::

### Worked exam interpretation

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **Question.** Select one recorded Shark Tank pitch at random. $D$
is the event of an on-air deal, and $L$ is the event of a late season
(Seasons 9 to 16). A student sees $P(D\mid L)=0.688$ and writes, "68.8% of deal
pitches came from late seasons." Explain what is wrong and give the correct
interpretation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model answer

The calculation conditions on $L$, so the denominator is the 734 pitches in
Seasons 9 to 16. The correct interpretation is that 68.8% of late-season
records reached an on-air deal. The sentence the student wrote describes the
reversed conditional probability, $P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 57.3\%$. Neither quantity
measures completed investment or a causal season effect.
:::

### Check the AI

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} You asked an AI assistant: "If a pitch got a deal, how likely is it that it came from a late season?" It answered:

> "68.8% of late-season pitches got a deal. So if a pitch got a deal, there is a 68.8% chance that it came from a late season."

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify
step of Attempt, Ask, Verify, Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

The AI turned the condition around. 68.8% is the share of deals among late-season pitches, 505 of 734. The question asks for the share of late-season pitches among deals: 505 of 882, about 57.3%. Always ask which group is in the denominator.
:::

### Make it yours

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Name one signal
it receives about customers or partners, for example a positive review, a
signed letter of intent, or a click on an ad. Sentence 1: which conditional
probability does the signal make you want to know? Write it with the
vertical bar and name the reference class. Sentence 2: which base rate would
you need to know before you trust the signal? There is no wrong answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See an example, then write your own

Take a student-run venture that sells boxes of prepared meals on campus. "I want $P(\text{becomes a paying customer} \mid \text{clicked the ad})$, where the reference class is the students who clicked the ad this month. Before I trust a high number of clicks, I would need the base rate of buyers among all students who saw the ad. With a very low base rate, most students who click still never buy."

@fig-b04-ad-tree shows why, with invented numbers. Suppose 2% of the students who see the ad become buyers. Half of the buyers click the ad, and 5% of the other students click it too. Of 1,000 students, 20 are buyers and 10 of them click. Of the 980 others, 49 click. So only $10/59\approx 17\%$ of the students who click become buyers, and about 83% of the clicks come from students who never buy.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b04-ad-tree
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-cap: "Tree of counts for 1,000 imaginary students who see the ad (invented numbers). Orange boxes are the students who click: 10 + 49 = 59 in total, of which only 10 become buyers, so P(buyer | click) = 10/59, about 17%."
#| fig-alt: "A tree that starts with 1,000 students, splits into 20 buyers and 980 non-buyers, and then into clicked and no click: 10 clicked and 10 no click among buyers, 49 clicked and 931 no click among non-buyers. The 10 and 49 clicked boxes are highlighted in orange, with 59 clicks in total."
# draw_count_tree() is defined in the code of the tree of 1,000 pitches
draw_count_tree(
  root = "1,000", root_label = "students",
  mid = c("20", "980"), mid_labels = c("buyer", "no buyer"),
  ends = c("10", "10", "49", "931"),
  end_labels = c("clicked", "no click", "clicked", "no click"),
  branch_labels = c("2% buy", "98% do not", "50% click", "50% not",
                    "5% click", "95% not"),
  side_text = "59\nclicked\nin total"
)
```
:::

for your signal with numbers you consider realistic.
